newsitem.title: GERMANY: Flood damage may boost intra-E.Europe farm trade.
newsitem.headline: Flood damage may boost intra-E.Europe farm trade.

text.p: Widespread flooding in eastern Europe has damaged crops and may raise import demand later this year, government and trade sources said on Monday.
Intra-regional trade in grain and oilseeds may help ease local shortages and dampen western sales hopes, but it also means there may be fewer net exports than previously expected.
"Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia may each lose 500,000 tonnes of grain, but there have not been any import requests logged here," a west European analyst said.
He said Poland might seek to buy up to 1.5 million tonnes of grain, especially high quality, if its crop fell to 23-24 million tonnes from earlier forecasts of 24.5 million.
Eastern German states might be able to supply some wheat but they would face competition from Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria with lower quality grain at cheaper price.
Traders believed those three countries plus Ukraine and Russia would be luckier with their grain crops than their neighbours and that weather patterns supported that view.
Earlier trade expectations that eastern Europe might supply 15 million tonnes of grain to the world market might be reduced if material stayed within the region.
A Polish analyst put grain losses at between 500,000 and 800,000 tonnes, which would reduce Poland's output to 23.6-24.7 million tonnes, versus domestic demand of 26.2 million.
Reserves are estimated at four million tonnes.
Two weeks of severe flooding and torrential rain have also hampered harvests in the southeast of the Czech Republic, where June estimates put the 1997 crop at seven million tonnes.
The Agricultural Chamber said on Monday the harvest estimate had been trimmed by 500,000 tonnes and that a further 200,000-500,000 might still be lost.
Consumption was forecast at 6.5 million tonnes and some 1.3 million are in stock.
Fears of further flooding in southern Poland eased on Tuesday and river levels in the Czech Republic were also falling.
Grain brokers in Hamburg said eastern Europe appeared to be clarifying import needs only slowly bcause its priority was to get supplies and services back on track.
Poland's rapeseed crop in 1997 might fall to 350,000-370,000 tonnes versus earlier forecasts of 400,000, private and public sector sources have said.
While this presented opportunities for western European suppliers, Ukraine and Russian sunseed and rapeseed would present competition.
Rapeseed producers in the Czech Republic had been expecting a 50,000-60,000 tonne export surplus, which could have gone to Poland, but this might not now be achieved.
Poland had failed so far to remove or reduce a 15 percent import tariff on rapeseed applied from July 1 in order to boost the local market, western traders noted.
There was talk that Poland might need to import 350,000-400,000 tonnes of rapeseed from late 1997 at the latest, of which Canada might supply 150,000 tonnes.
